hook.support: An ad for a drink shows friends at the beach, laughing. It doesn’t say much about the drink. Why? Because it’s selling a feeling. Learn to spot how.
hook.core: The ad shows mates on a beach at sunset, laughing, with a can in hand. It tells you almost nothing about the drink. That’s not an accident. Most ads aren’t selling a product; they’re selling a feeling. Once you can see how they do it, you can decide for yourself.
hook.extend: Ads work on two levels: what they say, and what they make you feel. Pictures, layout and words link a product or cause with a feeling or value. Reading an ad critically means taking those choices apart. Then you judge if they work, and for whom.

why.support: Ads try to get your money or your time. Knowing their tricks helps you choose.
why.core: You see hundreds of ads a day. Knowing how they work helps you make your own choices, and make better ads yourself.
why.extend: Judging ads is a work skill and a life skill. You’ll use it in marketing jobs, as a shopper and as a citizen.

articles.title: Selling a feeling

body.support:
An **ad** is made to get you to do something. Buy, join, click or care.

**Ask: who is it for?** The **target audience** is the people an ad is made for. Look at the people in it. Look at the place and the music.

**Ask: what feeling is it selling?** Ads often sell a feeling, not a product. This is called an **appeal**.
- **Belonging:** you’ll fit in.
- **Fun:** you’ll have a good time.
- **Fear:** something bad might happen.
- **Status:** people will look up to you.
.
**Look at the pictures.** A **visual cue** is a picture or colour that sends a message.
- Bright colours can mean fun.
- Dark colours can mean serious.
- Smiling faces can mean happy.
.
**Look at the words.**
- A **slogan** is a short, catchy line.
- A **call to action** tells you what to do. “Buy now.”.

Then ask: does it work? Would it get you to act?
body.core:
An **ad** is made to get its audience to act: buy, join, click, donate or change what they do.

**1. Who is it for?** Every ad has a **target audience**. Clues: the age and look of the people in it, the setting, the music, and where the ad appears (TikTok? the AFL? a bus stop?).

**2. What feeling is it selling?** Ads link a product or cause with a feeling. This is the **appeal**:
- **belonging:** “people like you use this”.
- **fun or humour:** you’ll enjoy it, and remember the ad.
- **fear:** something bad could happen if you don’t act.
- **status:** this will make you look successful.
- **values:** family, freedom, fairness, mateship.

**3. How do the visuals do it?** **Visual cues** do most of the work, often before you read anything:
- colour: warm and bright for fun, dark for serious.
- faces and body language: who looks happy, and why?
- layout: what’s biggest, and where does your eye go first?
- light and setting: sunset beach, city at night, family kitchen.

**4. What do the words do?** Look for the headline, the **slogan** and the **call to action**. Check the fine print.

**5. Is it effective?** An ad is **effective** if it gets its audience to act. Ask: what did the makers want? How would they know if it worked? Who might it not work for?
body.extend:
An **ad** is a promotional text designed to move a **target audience** to act: to buy, join, donate, click or change behaviour. Most ads persuade less through information than through association. They link a product or cause with a feeling or a set of **values**.

**Inferring the audience.** Clues include the people represented (age, style, lifestyle), the setting, music, language register and placement (the platform or time slot).

**Appeals.** Common appeals are belonging, humour, fear, status, aspiration and values such as mateship, family, freedom or fairness. Public-health ads often choose between fear and humour, and the choice affects who responds.

**Visual cues and layout.**
- **colour and light:** warm or cool, bright or dark.
- **composition:** what is largest, centred or in focus; where the eye goes first.
- **people:** facial expression, gaze (at you, or at the product?) and body language.
- **typography and logo placement**.

**Language.** Headlines, **slogans** (rhythm, rhyme, repetition), direct address (“you”), and the **call to action**. Note what the fine print says, and what it doesn’t.

**Evaluating effectiveness.** An ad’s appeal is not the same as its effect. Ask what its purpose was, what evidence there is that it worked, and who supplied that evidence. Results reported by the organisation that paid for the ad deserve a second look.

caseStudies.title: Dumb Ways to Die

body.support:
In **November 2012**, **Metro Trains Melbourne** put out a video. It was called **Dumb Ways to Die**.

It had cute cartoon characters and a catchy song. The characters died in silly ways.

At the end, it showed the dumbest ways of all. Standing too close to the edge of a train platform. Crossing train tracks.

The ad didn’t use fear. It used **fun**. People shared it all over the world.

Metro said that after the ad, there were fewer **near misses** at stations. But some experts asked if those numbers were right.

An ad can be popular. That doesn’t always mean it changed what people did.
body.core:
In **November 2012**, **Metro Trains Melbourne** released **Dumb Ways to Die**. Most rail safety ads used fear: crashes, injuries, grieving families. This one used **humour**.

Cute cartoon characters died in silly ways, set to a catchy song. Only at the end did it show the real message: the dumbest ways to die are around trains. Standing on the platform edge. Driving around the boom gates. Crossing the tracks.

The video spread around the world and won top advertising awards in **2013**.

Metro reported a **20%** drop in near misses after the campaign. But even Metro said it was too early to be sure. Some people in the industry questioned the numbers, and later reports said near misses had gone up again.

So was it **effective**? It was hugely popular. Whether it changed behaviour is harder to prove.
body.extend:
In **November 2012**, **Metro Trains Melbourne** launched **Dumb Ways to Die**. Rail safety advertising usually relied on fear. This campaign used **humour** instead: cute animated characters dying in absurd ways, set to a catchy song, with the real message held back until the end. The dumbest ways to die are around trains.

The video spread worldwide and won major awards at Cannes in **2013**. It was later turned into a mobile game.

On effectiveness, the picture is less clear. Metro reported a **20%** fall in near misses, compared with the annual average. But a Metro spokesperson said it was too early to be confident the change would last. An awards judge noted gaps between claimed and actual results. Later reporting suggested near misses had risen again.

The case shows the difference between **appeal** (how much people liked and shared it) and **effect** (whether behaviour changed). Most of the evidence for effect came from the organisation that paid for the campaign.

model.text:
**Ad:** a sports drink ad on YouTube, before a basketball video.
**Who it’s for:** teens who play sport. It shows young players at a local court.
**The feeling:** being a winner, and being part of a team.
**Visuals:** the player hits a shot in slow motion. Blue and white colours look cool and fresh. The bottle is in the team’s hands at the end.
**Words:** the slogan “Earn it” makes the drink feel like a reward for hard work.
**Does it work?** For sporty teens, yes: it’s exciting and short. But it never says what is in the drink. I’d want the facts before I buy.

teacher.overview: Students learn to read promotional material critically: infer the target audience, name the appeal (belonging, fun, fear, status, values), analyse visual cues, layout and language (headline, slogan, call to action, fine print), and evaluate appeal versus effect. The case study is Metro Trains Melbourne’s Dumb Ways to Die (2012), a hugely popular humour-based safety campaign whose reported safety results were questioned. The final task is a written breakdown of a real ad.
prep: Collect 4–6 current ads (print, video, social) across products and causes.
Check that the Dumb Ways to Die video is accessible on your network.
Avoid alcohol and gambling ads for younger students; check school policy.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 image as visual cue (fun, freedom, belonging); 2 short bold headline; 3 product small, feeling big; 4 catchy slogan; 5 call to action; 6 fine print with the facts and warnings.

**Sort:** feeling — “Live loud”; “join millions”; “your family deserves the best”. Fact — 80 mg caffeine; battery up to 20 hours (note “up to”); stand behind the yellow line.

**Case study:** purpose was to reduce risky behaviour around trains; humour rather than fear; aimed at young people (cartoon style, catchy song, shared online); Metro reported a 20% drop in near misses, but said it was too early to be sure, an awards judge noted gaps, and later reports suggested a rise. Popular is not the same as effective.

realityCheck: **Dumb Ways to Die shows cartoon deaths.** It’s mild, but warn students first, and be aware of any recent rail incidents in your community.
**Students love picking apart ads.** The challenge is getting past “it’s cringe” to how and why. The five questions keep them on task.
**Effectiveness claims are contested.** The course presents Metro’s figures and the doubts; don’t present either as settled.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Sound-off viewing is a strong hook.

levels.core: Aimed at about Years 5–6 reading: the standard version with audience, appeals, visual cues and a verdict.
levels.extend: Aimed at about Year 7 and up: values, composition, appeal versus effect, and the source of evidence.
